name: AI Hackathon
location: Multi-region via Yarl IT Hub (Uki Batticaloa, Uki Kilinochchi, Uki Jaffna) or individual Maha Vidyalayams
observation: The schooling system in Sri Lanka is fundamentally broken due to its lack of application-based learning. Students are taught to memorise and regurgitate on exams, but not to think and create on their own. This sets them up for rigid government jobs and not starting companies, which is what the region needs to spur economic development.
rootCause: It's the age-old understanding that strong performance in A-Level examinations is necessary to go to university, and going deeper, that going to university is a prerequisite to success in tech in Sri Lanka. Students need to snap out of the mindset that their careers are over if they don't get into public universities. The education system is focused on exams, not real-world skills.
description: A short 2-day hackathon: roughly half a day teaching students about using LLMs to build a business plan, how to vibe-code a technical demo, and how to make a pitch deck. Students then spend roughly 1 day building their solutions to hyper-local challenges — rationing of rice, farming schedules, water irrigation. The final half day is spent presenting in a friendly pitch competition. Aimed at high school students with no prior coding experience.
impactDescription: Practical short-term exposure to tools and entrepreneurial thinking that students can carry forward independently.
afterWeLeave: Students will know how to build demos on their own and likely start their own entrepreneurial journeys much sooner than they would have otherwise. Continuation would need Aram or a partner — potential paths include monthly follow-ups with new technical lessons as AI evolves, or partnering with Yarl IT Hub for ongoing inter-school competitions.
similarTried: Yarl IT Hub has students working on technical projects already but these are marathons over months, not sprints. There is value in a short intensive programme given how fast AI is moving. Aggash ran a similar event in Toronto and it worked really well as a first-pass intro to these tools.

phases.preTrip: Get intros to school principals/IT departments and lock down dates. Recruit mentors and judges. Put the content together.
phases.onTrip: One day of lessons to students. Supervise and provide feedback as they work on ideas. Run a pitch competition.
phases.postTrip: Monthly follow-ups with new technical lessons (e.g. AI agents) as technology evolves. Partner with YIH to run ongoing, larger inter-school competitions.

logisticsNeeded: Students need access to laptops and internet for the duration of the hackathon. Will stick to free tools. Ideally pair students with mentors for guidance — local entrepreneurs preferred, Aram team as backup. At least a few entrepreneurs as judges to inspire students. This is a 2-day event.
partnersNeeded: Yarl IT Hub is one option — could be facilitated very easily. High schools would be a better demographic. Getting intros to principals/IT departments at schools is the biggest challenge.
resources: Aggash can do the legwork with the sector lead. Need mentors and judges on the day — ~5 Aram team members as backup. Prizes as incentive (budget TBC).
successMetrics: 30-100 students completing the programme and 100% of them building a technical demo without prior technical experience.
risks: Language barrier — LLMs primarily use English, so explaining technical concepts and having students interact without enough English exposure won't be simple (Aggash can speak Tamil). Recruiting local mentors may be a challenge — may need to defer to Aram team. Getting intros/buy-in from school principals/IT departments is the biggest but most solvable challenge.
nextSteps: Get intros to school principals/IT departments. Recruit mentors and judges. Build the workshop content.

name: Telemedicine Pilot
observation: Patients in the Batticaloa region face significant barriers accessing hospital care, including poor road infrastructure and long travel distances. Many are on waiting lists for appointments they struggle to physically attend. With the current fuel crisis, doctors are also struggling to get to hospitals, further highlighting the need for digital healthcare pathways.
rootCause: Geographic isolation combined with an overstretched hospital system. Poor road infrastructure makes travel to hospital appointments difficult, costly, and time-consuming — particularly for those with mobility limitations or chronic conditions requiring frequent follow-up. This results in missed appointments, delayed diagnoses, and pressure on in-person capacity. There is no existing digital pathway for patients to access care remotely. The barrier is structural, not clinical.
description: Design and pilot a telemedicine system at RDHS Hospital, Batticaloa, enabling doctors to conduct remote consultations with patients who would otherwise struggle to attend in person. The pilot will establish a central technology hub in a rural area that connects with the hospital. The first step is to define clinical suitability criteria for remote appointments, and collect structured data on outcomes, patient satisfaction, time saved, and technical performance. The goal is to produce a technical report with findings and recommendations that the hospital can use to scale or adapt the model independently.
impactDescription: Addressing root structural causes with a long-term, sustainable digital healthcare solution that the hospital can own and scale.
afterWeLeave: The hospital will have a functioning telemedicine system, trained staff, and a technical report documenting what worked and what improvements are needed. If the pilot is successful, RDHS can continue and scale the service independently using the platform and workflows designed during the pilot. The initiative is structured for local ownership: the platform is hospital-managed, doctors receive training, and results are owned by the institution.
similarTried: A recent study assessed satisfaction of urban patients using telehealth during the Covid-19 pandemic in Sri Lanka. A private health insurance company has successfully implemented a telemedicine hub. No equivalent has been tried in the Batticaloa region with public hospital infrastructure.

phases.preTrip: Online kick-off meeting with RDHS to define scope, clinical suitability criteria, and patient recruitment pathway. Design qualitative, quantitative, and binary data collection surveys. Select and configure the telemedicine platform. Seek hospital approval and align on timelines and ethical requirements. Prepare doctor and patient training materials. Source equipment and confirm internet connectivity at site.
phases.onTrip: Set up technology hub at RDHS Hospital and run final connectivity tests. Train participating doctors on the platform and consultation process. Launch study: run remote appointments with recruited patients. Administer surveys to doctors and patients after each session. Meeting with RDHS leadership to present initial findings.
phases.postTrip: Compile technical report with all data. Present recommendations for scale/adaptation. Hand over platform and documentation to hospital for independent continuation.

logisticsNeeded: Requires dedicated time at RDHS Hospital — likely 2–3 full days for setup, staff training, and running initial appointments. A central technology hub must be set up with appropriate devices and internet connectivity. Need to identify and brief participating doctors, ensure a patient recruitment pathway is in place. Meeting with RDHS leadership after study to convey findings.
partnersNeeded: Primary partner: RDHS (Regional Director of Health Services), Batticaloa. Need sign-off on trial design, clinical scope, and patient recruitment pathway. Also need buy-in from participating doctors and hospital IT staff for technology setup.
resources: 2–3 volunteers with technology, healthcare, and data skills. Video-capable devices (tablets/laptops). Survey forms (qualitative and quantitative). Database or spreadsheet for results. Doctor training materials. Internet connectivity monitoring equipment. Budget: modest — primarily for devices if not provided by hospital, and local logistics.
successMetrics: Binary: appointments took place on time; no critical technical failures; patients joined successfully. Quantitative: average travel time saved per patient; average appointment length; number of appointments completed; internet speed during sessions. Qualitative: patients and doctors rate ease of joining as 4/5 or above; majority say they would use the service again. Ultimately: a completed technical report with data sufficient to inform whether and how to scale.
risks: Poor internet connectivity — will test speeds in advance and identify backup connection (e.g. mobile data). High patient recruitment volume — struggling to manage workflow. Technical issues during appointments — basic troubleshooting guide and designated tech support volunteer. Doctors not confident using platform — short training session in pre-launch phase. Patient needing emergency care — have access to transportation.
nextSteps: Kick-off meeting with RDHS to define scope. Design data collection surveys. Select and configure telemedicine platform. Source equipment and confirm connectivity.

name: Diaspora Identity & Intergenerational Storytelling
location: Multi-region — any location with groups willing to engage in conversations
observation: Many individuals come into the Aram experience with a limited or fragmented understanding of their own identity as Tamil diaspora members. There is no structured space before, during, or after the trip to process what this means personally. Many lack knowledge of family histories shaped by migration and war. Sensitive topics like war, displacement, and cultural loss are avoided or discussed superficially. Opportunities for intergenerational dialogue are limited despite being central to understanding identity.
rootCause: Many diaspora Tamil families are shaped by histories of conflict, displacement, and migration, leading to silence around the past — due to trauma, desire to protect younger generations, or cultural norms around emotional expression. There's a lack of intentional spaces for identity exploration. An intergenerational gap in language, cultural context, and lived experience makes meaningful engagement difficult. Even when desire is there, many don't know how to ask the right questions or navigate sensitive topics.
description: A structured, three-phase programme supporting participants in exploring Tamil identity through guided workshops, intergenerational oral history conversations, and facilitated reflection spaces. Participants conduct a short interview with a family or community member before the trip, engage in small group discussions during the trip, and produce a tangible post-trip output (written, audio, or creative) reflecting their evolving understanding of identity. These outputs contribute to a wider digital archive or exhibition.
impactDescription: Creating a lasting shift in how participants engage with their own identity, with tools and outputs that persist and grow beyond any single trip.
afterWeLeave: Participants are equipped with tools and confidence to continue intergenerational conversations independently. Archives preserve stories that would otherwise be lost — a resource that grows over time. The core elements — storytelling, reflection, dialogue — are inherently transferable and don't depend on Aram's continued presence.
similarTried: Nothing on the Aram website focuses specifically on identity exploration or intergenerational storytelling. Past initiatives involve reflection and community engagement, but none provide a structured framework for exploring Tamil identity or documenting family histories.

phases.preTrip: Develop pre-trip workshops and reflection materials on identity and intergenerational storytelling. Create question bank for participants. Train facilitators/volunteers on guiding sensitive conversations. Set up technical resources. Communicate assignments to participants.
phases.onTrip: Conduct small-group guided reflection sessions using pre-prepared prompts. Hold intergenerational conversations with local elders/families. Capture stories through audio, notes, or creative exercises. Facilitate creative reflection workshops. Encourage participants to draft post-trip outputs.
phases.postTrip: Participants finalise creative outputs (art, writing, podcast, digital archive). Curate digital archive or exhibition in the UK. Collect participant feedback. Encourage continued intergenerational dialogue. Use outputs to inform future trips/workshops.

logisticsNeeded: Dedicated small group discussion spaces where participants feel safe. Access to local elders, families, or community members willing to participate. Multiple days: one for guided conversations, one for reflection workshops, one for group synthesis. Facilitators trained in moderating sensitive conversations.
partnersNeeded: Local community elders or families willing to share personal histories (via existing Aram contacts). Facilitators for small group discussions. Local organisations or cultural centres supporting intergenerational storytelling. Aram trip coordinators for scheduling.
resources: 2-3 facilitators/moderators trained in guiding sensitive conversations. 1-2 support volunteers. Recording devices or smartphones. Notebooks, pens, reflection guides. Optional art supplies. Laptops/tablets for digital archives. Budget: ~$50-100 for materials.
successMetrics: All participants complete pre-trip interview assignment. Active engagement in reflection sessions during trip. Each participant produces at least one post-trip output. A collection of family stories documented and preserved. Participants report greater awareness of personal and intergenerational identity.
risks: Community members not available — prepare multiple contacts with backups. Volunteer dropout — train extra person, create session scripts. Technical issues — multiple recording methods, written notes as fallback. Idea not resonating — optional formats, icebreakers to ease into sensitive conversations.
nextSteps: Develop workshop materials and question bank. Identify and train facilitators. Set up technical resources. Communicate pre-trip assignments to participants.

name: Apprenticeship & Entrepreneurship Programme
location: Northern Province (Jaffna, Kilinochchi, Mullaitivu, Vavuniya), Eastern Province (Batticaloa, Trincomalee)
observation: In Northern Sri Lanka, many young adults feel limited to a narrow set of 'acceptable' career paths (doctor, engineer, lawyer). There is a lack of exposure to entrepreneurship, business thinking, and alternative income pathways. Many young people lack awareness of how to start a business, there is little structured support for idea development, and financial independence feels inaccessible without formal careers or migration. High underemployment despite education. Informal businesses exist but lack scalability and structure. Very little international VC investment reaches the Northern Province.
rootCause: Cultural pressure towards traditional professions. Lack of entrepreneurial role models. Limited access to capital or financial literacy. Education systems focused on exams, not real-world skills.
description: Building on last year's Apprentice activity with a structured follow-up mentoring component. The concept involves a programme to expose youth to entrepreneurship, business thinking, and alternative career paths, with a post-trip mentoring period to maintain momentum. This is a DRAFT — the full idea is still being developed. Thushanth is also connecting with a researcher writing a paper on employment aspirations in Mannar.
impactDescription: Addressing root causes of limited economic opportunity by creating pathways to entrepreneurship and alternative careers.
similarTried: Aram ran an Apprentice-style activity on the 2024/2025 trip. Ideas and observations from that experience directly inform this initiative.
partnersNeeded: Vanni Hope, local schools/youth centres, DreamSpace, local SME owners and informal entrepreneurs.
openQuestions: What does the follow-up mentoring period look like — who mentors, how often, what structure? How do we measure viability of scaling up as an organisation supporting young entrepreneurs?
nextSteps: Complete template Parts 2-4. Speak to Chat about ideas from last year's trip. Connect with researcher on Mannar employment paper. Define follow-up mentoring structure.

name: HE Access, IT Workshops & Career Support
location: Multi-region, with particular focus on Nuwara Eliya and plantation communities
observation: Public spending on education in Sri Lanka has been persistently low — just 2% of GDP, falling to 1.2% in 2022. Only 25.4% of people qualifying for higher education gain admission to public universities. Only 20% of students from low-income families complete secondary education compared to 70% from higher-income families. Plantation communities in Nuwara Eliya are among the poorest with the lowest enrollment rates. 17.5% of qualifying students pursue HE abroad, creating brain drain.
rootCause: Limited capacity of state universities (18 public vs 27 private). Rural-urban disparities in educational infrastructure and teaching quality. Reliance on private tutoring. Lack of infrastructure — during Covid, rural and plantation communities suffered most. Only 23% of college-age Sri Lankans enrolled in programmes employers value. Only 27% of women studied STEM, with most choosing biological sciences over engineering/maths.
description: Multiple possible directions still being explored: scholarships or partnerships with local HEIs in Sri Lanka; IT workshops specifically focused on women addressing the gender gap in STEM; career workshops and CV workshops. The idea needs narrowing — is it scholarships, workshops, or a combined approach?
impactDescription: Addressing structural barriers to education access, particularly for women and plantation communities.
afterWeLeave: Quantitative goal: 10-20 students gaining HEI access through grants/scholarships. Qualitative: improved student satisfaction and wellbeing.
similarTried: Aram has previously run CV workshops and IT workshops on trips.
logisticsNeeded: Connections with HEI professors and governance. Wifi and computers. Local and educational charities. Education government officials.
partnersNeeded: Local higher education institutions (TBC). Educational charities. Government education officials.
successMetrics: 10-20 students gaining HEI access. Student satisfaction and general wellbeing improvements.
openQuestions: Should this focus on scholarships, workshops, or both? Which HEIs to partner with? What's the specific target demographic — plantation communities, women in STEM, or broader?
nextSteps: Narrow the scope — decide between scholarships, workshops, or combined approach. Identify HEI partners. Complete remaining template sections.

name: Community Development Council (CDC)
location: Hill country (potential pilot at Mokra Estate); Vanni Hope as consultative partner
observation: Communities across Sri Lanka often lack structured mechanisms for identifying their own development needs and channelling resources toward solutions. External organisations tend to deliver projects top-down, creating dependency rather than local ownership. People are fixed into mindsets about viable careers, many places lack basic needs, and acquiring rights with government support remains a challenge. At the same time, some local leaders have successfully created development initiatives in partnership with external bodies — suggesting potential for community-led governance.
rootCause: Lack of local governance structures at community level that can identify needs, articulate them as proposals, and manage implementation. External aid often bypasses community agency. Without structured community engagement, development projects don't reflect actual priorities and aren't sustained after funders leave.
description: Establish Community Development Councils — elected groups of 10–15 local members (at least 50% women, at least 3 under 30) — who engage their community to identify issues, write project proposals, and implement solutions. Aram's role would be as 'Council Managers': supporting elections, training CDC members in community engagement, proposal writing, financial management, project implementation, monitoring, and accountability. Aram would select and fund proposals, releasing funds in increments at project milestones. CDCs would handle community engagement, proposal development, implementation, progress reporting, and post-implementation evaluation.
impactDescription: Creating a permanent local governance structure for community-led development that persists beyond any single trip or funder.
afterWeLeave: If successful, the community has an elected, trained body capable of identifying needs, writing proposals, managing projects, and reporting on outcomes independently. The CDC structure could eventually seek funding from other sources including the World Bank, government agencies, and other NGOs.
similarTried: Vanni Hope runs a cooperative model that involves training community members — learnings on what worked, challenges, and conflict resolution should inform this design.
logisticsNeeded: The drafted implementation plan spans 9+ weeks (introduction, elections, training, needs assessment, proposal writing, implementation, evaluation) which far exceeds the 2-week trip. Resolving how this maps onto the trip window is a critical question.
partnersNeeded: Vanni Hope (to consult on cooperative model learnings). Two women at Mokra Estate who are keen to lead. Local government relationship to be mapped.
openQuestions: How do we ensure CDCs report and evaluate after completion? What is the relationship between a CDC and local government? How do we approach training respectfully of people's time? How can we ensure equitable participation, not just representation? How can we measure sustainability? How does a 9-week plan fit a 2-week trip?
nextSteps: Fill the initiative planning template. Speak to Vanni Hope about their cooperative model. Connect with Mokra Estate contacts. Resolve the trip-timeline question.

name: Mokra Estate Community Pilot
observation: The CDC model needs a real-world test site — a defined community small enough to pilot with, but with enough local leadership appetite to sustain it. Plantation estate communities in the hill country are among the most disadvantaged in Sri Lanka with some of the lowest education, health, and economic indicators.
rootCause: Same structural issues as the CDC idea — lack of local governance mechanisms. Plantation communities face additional challenges: historical marginalisation, geographic isolation, and limited access to government services.
description: Test the Community Development Council model in a small, defined community. Mokra Estate has around 100–200 people and two local women already keen to support community development initiatives — making it a natural first pilot site for the CDC framework.
impactDescription: Piloting a replicable model of community-led governance in one of the most disadvantaged community types.
afterWeLeave: If the pilot works, Mokra has a functioning CDC. The learnings inform whether and how to replicate the model in other communities.
partnersNeeded: Two women at Mokra Estate (contacts to be obtained from Chat). Linked to Vanni Hope consultation from CDC idea.
nextSteps: Get contact details for the two women at Mokra from Chat. Scope whether the estate has the right conditions — community readiness, existing structures, resources, appetite. Directly linked to CDC idea above.

name: Diaspora Workshops & Debates (UK + SL)
observation: There is a disconnect between the Tamil diaspora in the UK and communities in Sri Lanka. Many diaspora members have limited understanding of the current situation on the ground, and people in Sri Lanka have limited exposure to diaspora perspectives. The sector vision for Diaspora Reconnection emphasises running events that bring together diaspora and Sri Lankan stakeholders.
rootCause: Geographic distance, generational gaps, and lack of structured forums for meaningful exchange. Most diaspora engagement is either purely financial (remittances, donations) or short-term visits without deep dialogue.
description: Run workshops, debates, and structured discussions that connect diaspora members with individuals in Sri Lanka. Both UK-based sessions (pre-trip) and Sri Lanka-based sessions (during trip), creating a platform for meaningful dialogue about shared identity, development priorities, and collaborative action.
impactDescription: Building relationships and creating structured spaces for genuine cross-border dialogue and understanding.
nextSteps: 1. Figure out logistics — how to run workshops/debates, target people involved. 2. Define the actual content and context for discussions. 3. Explore incentive criteria for participation.

name: Personal Sponsorship Scheme
observation: School children aged 6-10 in Sri Lanka face barriers to educational access and basic needs. The diaspora has individuals willing to provide sustained support, but there's no structured mechanism connecting individual sponsors to individual children in a transparent, accountable, and sustainable way.
rootCause: Poverty and lack of resources at the family level. Existing aid is often institutional rather than individual, missing children who fall through the gaps of formal programmes.
description: A personal sponsorship scheme providing school children aged 6-10 with individualised help — potentially covering educational materials, basic needs, and ongoing support through a diaspora sponsor.
impactDescription: Direct, tangible support to individual children through sustained diaspora connections.
nextSteps: 1. Define long-term and short-term goals — end goal, target audience, specific individuals. 2. Budget/logistics/media required for the sponsorship. 3. What needs to happen within the next 2 weeks.

name: SEN Buddy / Friendship Sessions
location: Near SEN homes; partner with local schools
observation: Most people only ever interact with individuals with special needs if they have a sibling or cousin with a disability. There's an awkwardness or stigma that won't go away because of lack of exposure. SEN children in homes have limited social interaction with the wider community, which doesn't prepare them for life beyond the home.
rootCause: Societal stigma and lack of exposure. Mainstream communities rarely interact with SEN individuals, perpetuating ignorance and discomfort. SEN homes can become isolated environments rather than integrated parts of the community.
description: Get a group of teenagers (14-18 year olds) and bring them together with SEN kids and young adults for a 'Social & Friendship' session. Pair them up for creative activities — learn a dance, paint, something collaborative. End with a shared meal like normal friends. Extension: incorporate local community youth who can continue the same activities after Aram leaves, creating sustainable community integration rather than a one-off Aram activity.
impactDescription: Building genuine friendships and breaking down stigma, with a pathway to sustained community integration through local youth involvement.
afterWeLeave: If local youth are involved rather than just Aram volunteers, the buddy sessions can continue independently. The participating teenagers carry a changed perspective into adulthood.
partnersNeeded: Local schools or existing SEN organisations to source teenage participants.
nextSteps: Partner with local schools or existing SEN organisations. Design session structure — activities, pairing method, facilitation. Explore whether this can be a recurring local programme.

name: Media Documenting
observation: Aram's work across trips generates significant stories and impact, but documentation has been inconsistent. Good documentation serves accountability to donors/partners, website and social media content, internal learning, and volunteer recruitment for future years.
rootCause: No dedicated media/documentation role or strategy in previous trips. Documentation happened ad hoc, meaning important moments were missed and content quality varied.
description: A dedicated media documenting effort across the trip — potentially covering video, photography, social media content, and/or internal documentation of activities and impact.
impactDescription: Cross-cutting support for all sectors by capturing and communicating their work effectively.
openQuestions: Is this video production, photography, social media, internal documentation, or all of the above? What's the output — a trip documentary, social media posts, website content, donor reports?
nextSteps: Define scope and output format. Determine equipment and skills needed.

name: Drug Awareness Programme
observation: Drug usage is one of the social issues undermining societal progress in the communities Aram works with, often to a much greater extent than in the past. Substance abuse among young people is a growing concern. The Wellbeing sector vision lists a drug awareness and education programme as a planned initiative.
rootCause: Root causes need research — the Wellbeing sector vision asks 'What are the root causes and prevalence of substance abuse among young people?' Likely factors include post-conflict trauma, limited economic opportunity, lack of recreational alternatives, and social disengagement.
description: A drug awareness and education programme targeting young people in the communities Aram visits. Format still to be defined — could be workshops, peer education, community awareness campaigns, or integration with sports/creative activities.
impactDescription: Directly addressing a growing social issue through awareness and education, with potential for deeper systems change if combined with alternative engagement programmes.
nextSteps: Research existing drug awareness programmes in Sri Lankan communities. Define target audience and format. Consider combining with Alakki's sports/martial arts idea for a dual awareness + action approach.

name: Infrastructure for Wellbeing / Social Spaces
observation: Many communities in the regions Aram works with lack dedicated spaces for social gathering, recreation, and community wellbeing. Physical infrastructure for social connection is limited — few places for young people to gather, for community events, or for wellbeing support.
rootCause: Post-conflict and economically disadvantaged communities often prioritise basic survival needs over social infrastructure. The absence of gathering spaces contributes to isolation, limited social cohesion, and reduced mental wellbeing.
description: Creating physical social/community spaces that support wellbeing. Still at conceptual stage — could mean building or refurbishing a community space, equipping existing spaces with recreational materials, or creating mobile/pop-up social spaces.
impactDescription: Building community infrastructure for social connection, with potential for lasting impact if physical spaces are created.
nextSteps: 1. Research what community spaces currently exist. 2. Define what 'social spaces' means concretely. 3. Identify a specific community and location.

name: Diaspora Crowdfunding Platform
observation: The Tamil diaspora sends significant remittances and donations, but money is channelled informally without accountability, transparency, or strategic direction. There's no structured way for diaspora members to fund specific community projects, track impact, or connect with the people they're supporting.
rootCause: Lack of digital infrastructure connecting diaspora resources to community needs. Existing donation channels are opaque, one-directional, and don't create a feedback loop between funder and community.
description: A crowdfunding platform where diaspora members can browse community projects in Sri Lanka, fund specific initiatives, and track impact. Could integrate with Aram's own initiatives or operate as a broader platform for community-driven development.
impactDescription: Creating permanent digital infrastructure for transparent diaspora-to-community resource flow.
nextSteps: Chat to create a group chat for the working team. Define the MVP scope — minimum viable version that delivers value.

name: Practical Skills in Virtual Mentorship
location: Virtual (within existing Aram virtual mentorship programme)
observation: Aram's existing virtual mentorship platform connects diaspora professionals with young people in Sri Lankan children's homes. The current curriculum may not include enough practical, vocational, or life skills content — the kind of knowledge that directly translates into employability and independence.
rootCause: Academic education in Sri Lanka is heavily theoretical. Young people in children's homes may have even less access to practical skills development. The mentorship programme has an opportunity to fill this gap but needs curriculum design.
description: Add practical/vocational curriculum modules to the existing virtual mentorship programme — things like financial literacy, basic IT skills, communication skills, CV writing, interview preparation, or trade-specific knowledge.
impactDescription: Building sustained capability through the existing mentorship infrastructure, making it more practically relevant.
partnersNeeded: Existing virtual mentorship programme infrastructure and participants.
nextSteps: Define what curriculums should be taught — what skills are most in demand? Consult with mentors and home staff.

name: Videos & Leaflets on Optometry
observation: Eye health awareness and access to optometry services is limited in rural communities across Sri Lanka. Many people don't have access to basic eye health information or know when to seek care, particularly in upcountry and remote areas.
rootCause: Lack of accessible health education materials in local languages. Limited optometry services outside urban centres. Low awareness of preventable eye conditions.
description: Create educational video and leaflet content on eye health (optometry) in formats accessible to rural communities — potentially in Tamil, covering common conditions, when to seek help, and preventive care. Content could be distributed through community partners, schools, or a centralised digital resource hub.
impactDescription: Directly providing health education that communities can access and reuse independently.
nextSteps: 1. Decide what video topics to cover. 2. Explore different content delivery methods. 3. Investigate whether this can be part of a centralised Aram resource hub.

name: Optom for SEN — Orange Tent Therapy
observation: Children with special educational needs often have undiagnosed or unaddressed vision problems that compound their developmental challenges. Standard optometry services are not adapted for SEN children — the environment, communication approach, and assessment methods all need modification. Many SEN homes lack specialised staff to meet children's needs.
rootCause: SEN homes lack access to specialist healthcare services. Optometry services are not adapted for neurodivergent children. Staff are not trained to identify vision-related issues.
description: Bring adapted optometry support to SEN children — potentially using the 'Orange Tent Therapy' approach, which creates a controlled, calming sensory environment for eye assessments with children who might find standard clinical settings distressing.
impactDescription: Directly addressing an unmet healthcare need for some of the most vulnerable children.
partnersNeeded: SEN homes (TBC which ones would benefit most).
openQuestions: Does this need a qualified optometrist on the trip team?
nextSteps: Research costs and expertise needed. Identify which SEN homes would benefit most.

name: SEN Safe Spaces & Belonging
observation: Children in orphanages and SEN homes often live in environments that don't fully support their emotional, sensory, or developmental needs. Infrastructure in many SEN homes is inadequate. Staff burnout and lack of motivation is a factor — there's no dedicated space for staff either.
rootCause: Under-resourcing of children's homes. Lack of understanding of how physical environments affect emotional regulation, sensory processing, and sense of belonging. Staff are undervalued and lack their own supportive infrastructure.
description: A multi-layered approach: understand children's needs through participatory methods (getting them to draw/express what they want), then create calming-down zones or enclosed spaces for emotional regulation, sensory-appropriate spaces for SEN children, and dedicated staff wellbeing spaces. Design incentive systems for keeping spaces well maintained after creation.
impactDescription: Physical infrastructure improvements that persist, combined with a needs-first approach that understands before imposing solutions.
partnersNeeded: Orphanages and SEN homes (specific ones TBC).
openQuestions: What's feasible within a 2-week trip — design or build or both? How to incentivise ongoing maintenance?
nextSteps: Research participatory design methods for working with children. Consider both children's spaces and staff spaces. Scope feasibility within trip timeframe.

name: Sports/Martial Arts for Substance Abuse Intervention
observation: Substance abuse among young people is a growing issue. Drug usage is undermining societal progress to a much greater extent than in the past. Sports and physical activity are recognised globally as effective interventions for at-risk youth — providing structure, community, discipline, and healthy outlets.
rootCause: Post-conflict trauma, limited economic opportunity, lack of recreational alternatives, social disengagement, and absence of structured youth programmes. Young people with nothing to do and no positive outlets are most vulnerable.
description: Establish substance abuse intervention programmes through sports and martial arts centres. Could mean setting up regular training sessions, establishing clubs, or partnering with existing facilities for structured programmes targeting at-risk youth.
impactDescription: Creating sustained programmes that address root causes of substance abuse through positive engagement and community structure.
nextSteps: Research existing sports/martial arts facilities. Define target community and model. Consider combining with Avi's Drug Awareness Programme for dual awareness + action approach.

name: Community Book Exchange
observation: Access to books and reading materials is limited in many communities Aram works with. Libraries are scarce, and the education system's focus on textbooks and exams means reading for personal development is not a norm.
rootCause: Lack of community-level infrastructure for knowledge sharing. Limited access to diverse reading materials beyond school textbooks. No culture of community resource exchange.
description: A book exchange programme connecting communities — potentially through physical book-sharing points, community libraries, or a rotating collection system between partner organisations and homes.
impactDescription: Building community connections through shared resources and a culture of knowledge sharing.
nextSteps: Research what exists. Define scope — which communities, what kinds of books, physical infrastructure needed, how to sustain after setup.

name: Siblings Tech Network
observation: SEN advocacy in Sri Lanka is limited. The next generation of advocates will likely come from those closest to SEN individuals — their siblings. Many siblings are more tech-literate and could be mobilised for awareness, advocacy, and practical support.
rootCause: SEN advocacy infrastructure is weak. Siblings are an untapped resource — they understand challenges firsthand but have no structured way to contribute or connect with each other.
description: Set up a network of tech-oriented siblings of SEN individuals who can serve as on-the-ground SEN partners for next-generation advocacy — sharing information, raising awareness, providing peer support, and contributing to practical improvements using technology.
impactDescription: Building a self-sustaining advocacy network that grows independently over time.
nextSteps: Research feasibility. Identify potential first members. Define what 'tech-oriented' means in practice.

name: Staff Training at ORHAN
observation: Staff at SEN homes are undertrained and often don't have the skills to manage SEN behaviours or maximise children's developmental potential. Many teachers just look after kids rather than seeking to maximise their potential with a development path. ORHAN has been specifically identified as needing staff capacity building.
rootCause: Lack of access to SEN-specific training. No ongoing professional development infrastructure. Limited resources and equipment for evidence-based approaches.
description: Deliver staff training at ORHAN in partnership with Dr James. Launch in person during the trip, with setup (donated projector/laptop) sorted prior to arrival. Training should cover SEN behaviour management, developmental approaches, and practical strategies staff can implement independently.
impactDescription: Building permanent staff capability that improves care quality long after Aram leaves.
partnersNeeded: Dr James (for training content and delivery). ORHAN management.
resources: Donations needed: projector, laptop for ORHAN.
nextSteps: Contact Dr James to confirm scope and format. Source donations for projector/laptop setup. Design training materials that can be left behind as reference.

name: EHCPs at Serendip
observation: Children at SEN homes often lack individualised development plans. In the UK, Education, Health and Care Plans provide a structured framework for assessing needs and creating tailored support. Nothing equivalent exists at homes like Serendip. Numerous children have much higher capabilities than they are treated for — their potential is being underestimated without proper assessment.
rootCause: No framework for individual assessment and planning. Staff lack tools and training to evaluate children's capabilities systematically. Without individual plans, children receive generic rather than tailored support.
description: Adapt and pilot the EHCP model at Serendip — starting with trial reviews for 3 children on one of the Discovery/Research days. This would create a template and process that Serendip could continue using, and that could be replicated at other homes.
impactDescription: Introducing a replicable assessment and planning framework that ensures each child gets support matched to their actual capabilities.
openQuestions: How to adapt the UK EHCP framework for the Sri Lankan context? Who has the expertise to conduct the reviews?
nextSteps: Research EHCP process adaptation. Identify 3 children at Serendip for the trial. Design assessment tools and documentation templates.

name: Vocational Training for SEN
observation: SEN young people in homes face a cliff edge when they age out — with few vocational skills, limited social networks, and almost no pathway to employment or independent living. Engagement structures in homes seek to look after kids rather than maximise their potential with a development path.
rootCause: No structured transition planning for SEN young people ageing out of care. Care homes focus on day-to-day management rather than long-term outcomes. Limited understanding of what vocational options are realistic and available.
description: Research and develop vocational training pathways for SEN young people — understanding what jobs or activities they could realistically do, what training they'd need, and what support structures would make employment possible.
impactDescription: Creating long-term pathways to independence for SEN young people who currently face a cliff edge when ageing out of care.
openQuestions: What vocational options exist for SEN individuals in Sri Lanka? What's the legal/practical landscape for SEN employment?
nextSteps: Research vocational options and SEN employment landscape. Identify homes with young people approaching transition age. Consider what skills are both teachable and lead to actual local employment.
